![bug · high](https://img.shields.io/badge/bug-high-red)
`validateCalcifyLifecycle` only checks that the provided binding digest is well-formed; it never verifies that it matches the service's actual source profile hash. As written, any lowercase 64-char hex string will pass validation, and the processor will later emit lifecycle facts with a potentially unrelated `FiniteBindingDigest`, defeating the binding guarantee this mode is supposed to enforce.

**Suggestion:**
```suggestion
func validateCalcifyLifecycle(service *app.Service, enabled bool, binding string, batchSize int) error {
	if !enabled {
		return nil
	}
	decoded, err := hex.DecodeString(binding)
	if err != nil || len(decoded) != 32 || len(binding) != 64 || binding != strings.ToLower(binding) {
		return fmt.Errorf("Calcify lifecycle requires lowercase SHA256 finite binding digest")
	}
	if service == nil || service.CalcifySourceProfileHash() == "" {
		return fmt.Errorf("Calcify lifecycle requires finite source profile")
	}
	if err := service.ValidateCalcifySourceProfile(); err != nil {
		return err
	}
	if binding != service.CalcifySourceProfileHash() {
		return fmt.Errorf("Calcify lifecycle finite binding digest does not match source profile")
	}
	if batchSize != 1 {
		return fmt.Errorf("Calcify lifecycle requires batch size 1")
	}
	return nil
}
```

<!-- ocr-38068796768-2-01a08f18b2ef4570 -->
![bug · medium](https://img.shields.io/badge/bug-medium-orange)
`ProcessOnce` now fails fast when lifecycle mode is enabled, but `NewProcessor` is still used directly in tests and other package-internal call sites without going through `StartRunner`. That means a caller can construct a processor with `CalcifyLifecycleEnabled=true` and only discover the fatal config error on the first fetch path, which is a different contract from the runner-level gate and makes the mode easy to partially enable in code paths that expect `NewProcessor` to be usable immediately. Consider moving this validation into `NewProcessor` or making the constructor return an error so invalid lifecycle settings cannot escape initialization.

**Suggestion:**
```suggestion
func NewProcessor(service *app.Service, source CommandSource, publisher EventBatchPublisher, config ProcessorConfig) (*Processor, error) {
	// ... existing setup ...
	lifecycleError := validateCalcifyLifecycle(service, config.CalcifyLifecycleEnabled, config.CalcifyFiniteBindingDigest, config.BatchSize)
	if lifecycleError != nil {
		return nil, lifecycleError
	}
	processor := &Processor{ /* ... */ }
	if config.CalcifyLifecycleEnabled {
		processor.lifecycleProfileHash = service.CalcifySourceProfileHash()
	}
	return processor, nil
}
```

![bug · medium](https://img.shields.io/badge/bug-medium-orange)
This branch makes `StartRunner` unconditionally fail whenever `MATCHING_ENGINE_CALCIFY_LIFECYCLE_ENABLED=true`, even after validation succeeds. That means the feature can never actually be activated through the runtime entrypoint, so any deployment using the new config will see a hard startup failure rather than the intended gated mode. If this is only meant as a temporary block, it should be guarded more narrowly or moved behind an explicit migration flag.

**Suggestion:**
```suggestion
		// Model fact/capture proof cannot authorize replay under a new mode.
		// O2 replaces this gate only after durable registration and bound restore.
		return nil, fmt.Errorf("Calcify lifecycle live activation requires durable binding and restore (O2)")
```

![bug · high](https://img.shields.io/badge/bug-high-red)
`record.value()` can be null for tombstone messages, but this path converts it to an empty byte array and then attempts to parse it as a payload. That will fail later as an `IllegalArgumentException`, but it also means a tombstone is treated like malformed input rather than a recoverable no-op. If this topic can carry tombstones, we should handle them explicitly (for example, retain/skip according to the intended contract) instead of silently coercing to `byteArrayOf()`.

**Suggestion:**
```suggestion
        val payload = record.value()
        if (payload == null) {
            retain(state, byteArrayOf(), offset, resume, "null source record")
            return
        }
```

![bug · medium](https://img.shields.io/badge/bug-medium-orange)
`validateState()` allows `retainedSuffixCount > 0` only when `fault` is non-empty, but `initializeModel()` accepts a restored checkpoint without revalidating that the retained suffix history fits the available source window for the new cut. If the checkpoint is only partially covered by the new `availableEnd`, the processor can start from a state that cannot be safely replayed and later fail inconsistently. Consider tightening the restore preconditions against the retained suffix tail before returning the checkpoint.

**Suggestion:**
```suggestion
            is FiniteLifecycleStartCut.Restore -> {
                require(managed == null || managed == cut.checkpoint) { "managed/certified checkpoint mismatch" }
                val requiredEnd = maxOf(
                    cut.checkpoint.resumeOffset,
                    cut.checkpoint.retainedSuffixList.maxOfOrNull { it.resumeOffset } ?: binding.genesisOffset,
                )
                require(cut.availableBeginning <= binding.genesisOffset && cut.availableEnd >= requiredEnd) {
                    "required source history unavailable"
                }
                FiniteLifecycleReducer.validateState(cut.checkpoint, binding)
                cut.checkpoint
            }
```

![bug · medium](https://img.shields.io/badge/bug-medium-orange)
`canonical()` sorts the two parties before serializing them, which makes the budget digest independent of the buy/sell ordering in the binding. That means two bindings with the same participant/account pairs but opposite sides will produce the same canonical bytes even though `FiniteLifecycleBinding` treats the side assignment as semantically significant. If this digest is used as an identity input, it can collapse distinct bindings into the same hash.

**Suggestion:**
```suggestion
val ordered = parties.sortedWith(compareBy<FiniteParty> { it.participant }.thenBy { it.account })
            require(ordered.size == 2 && ordered.map { it.participant to it.account }.distinct().size == 2)
            out.writeInt(ordered.size)
            parties.forEach { out.frame(it.participant); out.frame(it.account); out.writeByte(when(it.side) {
```
